Professional context: Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW).
For cross-border work, establish legal responsibility explicitly; the selector does not decide it.

foundations.title: Professional Foundations — Victoria
foundations.action: Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task.
foundations.record: Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment. Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths. Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference. Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — Victoria
care-support.action: Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
care-support.record: Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate. Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme. Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision. For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria
mca.action: Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability.
mca.record: Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement. Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy. For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement. The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria
dols.action: Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies.
dols.record: For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions. Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply. Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction. OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.

mha.title: Mental Health — Victoria
mha.action: Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria.
mha.record: Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary. Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements. Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions. Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — Victoria
safeguarding.action: Hear the adult safely and identify immediate danger, coercion and practical dependence.
safeguarding.record: Identify whether the concern involves family violence, a disability or aged-care provider, another service or crime. Use the relevant specialist, police and regulatory routes, checking any mandatory reporting duty. Plan safe contact, practical support and follow-up without assuming that a referral authorises coercive action. Explain the appropriate complaint, advocacy or court route for the issue. OPA can provide information about decision-making and rights within its remit. Keep the adult’s wishes and the legal authority for any intervention visible, including where agencies disagree.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Victoria
children.action: Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty.
children.record: Report to Child Protection as soon as practicable where the duty is engaged, including new grounds arising later. Consider a support referral to The Orange Door where appropriate, without substituting it for a required protection report. Check separate police and organisational duties, and plan child participation, cultural support and continuity. Explain the Child Protection process and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. DFFH guidance distinguishes reporting routes from family-support referrals. Advice within an organisation should not delay an applicable personal reporting obligation.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Victoria
rights.action: Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority.
rights.record: Consider the actual impact, alternatives and any lawful basis for limiting a right. Arrange accessible and culturally safe participation and address applicable equality obligations. Check the relevant privacy regime and explain access, correction, complaints and review. The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission explains Charter duties and discrimination. Privacy and health complaints use their respective bodies and statutory routes. Obtain advice about the remedy for an alleged Charter breach rather than promising that every concern has a standalone Charter claim.

sources.title: Victoria Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task. Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment. Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths. Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating association membership, clinical experience or a job title with every statutory appointment.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment. Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate. Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme. Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating NDIS eligibility as approval for every requested service, or using obsolete aged-care programme rules.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: The Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 governs important medical-consent and advance-care-directive questions. The Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 provides a separate framework for guardianship, administration and supported appointments. Specify whether the decision concerns treatment, personal matters or finances. Medical decision-making capacity concerns understanding the relevant information and effects, retaining it for the decision, considering it when choosing, and conveying the choice and related views or needs by any workable means. Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An advance care directive can include an instructional directive and a values directive, with different effects. Where the person cannot make the treatment decision, identify the lawful medical treatment decision maker. Their task concerns the decision the person would have made, informed by relevant preferences and values, rather than simply the representative’s preferred outcome.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability. Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement. Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy. For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating an instructional directive as merely optional, or assuming financial administration includes medical consent.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Senior Practitioner publishes directions and prohibitions, including a permanent-prohibition notice dated September 2025. Check the current rules for the particular practice and cohort before considering an application. A prohibited practice is not made permissible by including it in a behaviour support plan.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies. For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions. Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply. Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating historical approval or a lodged plan as permanent permission, including for a prohibited practice.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 replaced the 2014 Act. It prefers voluntary assessment and treatment and provides separate assessment orders, temporary treatment orders and Mental Health Tribunal treatment orders. Each stage has its own authorised decision-maker and requirements.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Compulsory treatment criteria include mental illness; immediate treatment needed to prevent serious deterioration in health or serious harm; that treatment being provided if the order is made; and no reasonably available less restrictive means. Evidence that a service is actually available matters. Assessment-order criteria should not be replaced with the treatment-order test.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria. Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary. Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements. Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using the assessment and treatment criteria interchangeably or treating a support person as the treatment decision-maker.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: Adult concerns may require family-violence services, police, OPA, disability safeguards, aged-care oversight or a provider complaint. Identify the relationship and service setting before selecting a route. The Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is relevant to violence and abuse within its defined relationships; not every adult concern is governed by that framework.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Orange Door provides access to family-violence and family-support services. NDIS and aged-care providers have their own incident and regulatory obligations. A referral for support, a reportable incident and an application for a protective order are different actions.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Hear the adult safely and identify immediate danger, coercion and practical dependence. Identify whether the concern involves family violence, a disability or aged-care provider, another service or crime. Use the relevant specialist, police and regulatory routes, checking any mandatory reporting duty. Plan safe contact, practical support and follow-up without assuming that a referral authorises coercive action.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the appropriate complaint, advocacy or court route for the issue. OPA can provide information about decision-making and rights within its remit. Keep the adult’s wishes and the legal authority for any intervention visible, including where agencies disagree.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating all adult safeguarding as one statutory process or assuming a guardianship referral resolves family violence.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 distinguishes protection grounds and mandatory reporting. The mandatory-reporter categories depend on the role: do not assume every person called a social worker is included solely by title. A social worker may fall within a listed role, such as school counselling or out-of-home care work.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: DFFH guidance requires listed reporters who form the relevant reasonable belief in their work to report protection concerns involving physical injury or sexual abuse. Other forms of significant harm may also be reported. The child’s harm and parental protection must be considered; the statutory reporting duty is not identical to every possible wellbeing concern.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty. Report to Child Protection as soon as practicable where the duty is engaged, including new grounds arising later. Consider a support referral to The Orange Door where appropriate, without substituting it for a required protection report. Check separate police and organisational duties, and plan child participation, cultural support and continuity.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the Child Protection process and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. DFFH guidance distinguishes reporting routes from family-support referrals. Advice within an organisation should not delay an applicable personal reporting obligation.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming all social-work job titles create the same reporting duty, or confusing voluntary support with a mandatory report.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?
cards.answer: The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 requires covered public authorities to act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights, subject to statutory exceptions. Identify whether the provider is a public authority for the function involved. A Charter statement should explain the affected rights and reasoning, not simply declare compliance.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Equal Opportunity Act 2010, Health Records Act 2001 and Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 have different scopes. Commonwealth law may also apply. Determine the organisation and information involved before selecting a privacy or discrimination pathway.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority. Consider the actual impact, alternatives and any lawful basis for limiting a right. Arrange accessible and culturally safe participation and address applicable equality obligations. Check the relevant privacy regime and explain access, correction, complaints and review.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission explains Charter duties and discrimination. Privacy and health complaints use their respective bodies and statutory routes. Obtain advice about the remedy for an alleged Charter breach rather than promising that every concern has a standalone Charter claim.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming every private provider has identical Charter duties or that naming rights establishes proper consideration.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A practitioner is asked to sign a statutory assessment because they hold an AASW credential, without checking the specific appointment requirements.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Read the law and service procedure governing that assessment. Confirm qualifications, appointment and scope before signing. Bring any gap to the responsible manager and arrange an authorised practitioner while continuing work that is within your role.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person is told that their NDIS plan should pay for every need after a hospital admission, including treatment and unsuitable housing.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Map the actual support sought and the responsibility of each system. Obtain the relevant decisions and coordinate health, housing and disability support. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements rather than presenting an unfunded referral as a completed plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person’s advance directive refuses a particular treatment, but a relative asks the team to ignore it because they believe treatment would help.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check validity, applicability and whether the statement is an instructional or values directive. Involve the responsible clinician and obtain advice where the position is disputed. Do not substitute the relative’s preference for the legal effect of the document or the person’s own decision.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A provider proposes a restraint copied from an old plan and assumes approval can be renewed without checking current directions.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check whether the practice is now prohibited and whether the previous approval is relevant to the present circumstances. Assess alternatives and consult the responsible practitioner. Do not apply an obsolete approval to a new plan or bypass the Senior Practitioner’s requirements.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person is considered for a treatment order, but the proposed immediate treatment has not been arranged and a community alternative has not been explored.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check all criteria, including that treatment will be provided and whether a less restrictive means is reasonably available. Obtain the person’s preferences and supports. The existence of illness and concern about deterioration alone does not explain the whole order decision.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult with disability reports financial control by a partner and an unrelated failure by a support provider to deliver personal care.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the family-violence concern and provider failure separately while coordinating safety. Consider the specialist family-violence route and the appropriate provider or NDIS response. Arrange continuity of care and safe contact rather than assuming one agency will handle both matters.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A school counsellor receives a disclosure of physical harm, while a colleague says the family should first be referred for voluntary parenting support.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the reasonable-belief and protection conditions and make the required report if met. Assess immediate safety and follow any separate police duty. Parenting support can run alongside the protection response; it does not replace it.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Victoria
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A public service restricts all family visits for administrative convenience without considering a resident’s cultural and family relationships.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Identify the rights affected, the purpose of the restriction and realistic alternatives. Hear the resident and supporters they choose, consider the applicable legal duties and record the reasoning. Review the blanket policy’s effect on the individual rather than relying only on its general wording.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.

Local pathway:
Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task.
Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment.
Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths.
Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

Sources:
https://www.aasw.asn.au/about-aasw/ethics-standards/code-of-ethics/

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

Local pathway:
Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate.
Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme.
Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

Sources:
https://ndis.gov.au/applying/application-process/what-access-request-form
https://ndis.gov.au/ndis-laws/getting-ndis-back-track/summary-legislation-changes
https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/aged-care-act/resources/providers
https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/chsp/reforms

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 governs important medical-consent and advance-care-directive questions. The Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 provides a separate framework for guardianship, administration and supported appointments. Specify whether the decision concerns treatment, personal matters or finances. Medical decision-making capacity concerns understanding the relevant information and effects, retaining it for the decision, considering it when choosing, and conveying the choice and related views or needs by any workable means. Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.

An advance care directive can include an instructional directive and a values directive, with different effects. Where the person cannot make the treatment decision, identify the lawful medical treatment decision maker. Their task concerns the decision the person would have made, informed by relevant preferences and values, rather than simply the representative’s preferred outcome.

Local pathway:
Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability.
Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement.
Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy.
For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.

Sources:
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/your-rights/your-healthcare
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/interpreting-an-instructional-directive
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/medical-treatment-planning-and-decisions-act-2016
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/guardianship-and-administration-act-2019
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/patient-capacity-to-consent

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.

The Senior Practitioner publishes directions and prohibitions, including a permanent-prohibition notice dated September 2025. Check the current rules for the particular practice and cohort before considering an application. A prohibited practice is not made permissible by including it in a behaviour support plan.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies.
For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions.
Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply.
Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.

Sources:
https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/about-victorian-senior-practitioner
https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/victorian-senior-practitioners-directions-and-prohibitions
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/disability-act-2006
https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 replaced the 2014 Act. It prefers voluntary assessment and treatment and provides separate assessment orders, temporary treatment orders and Mental Health Tribunal treatment orders. Each stage has its own authorised decision-maker and requirements.

Compulsory treatment criteria include mental illness; immediate treatment needed to prevent serious deterioration in health or serious harm; that treatment being provided if the order is made; and no reasonably available less restrictive means. Evidence that a service is actually available matters. Assessment-order criteria should not be replaced with the treatment-order test.

Local pathway:
Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria.
Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary.
Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements.
Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-2022
https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/compulsory-assessment-and-treament
https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/treatments-and-interventions/treatment-orders

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Adult concerns may require family-violence services, police, OPA, disability safeguards, aged-care oversight or a provider complaint. Identify the relationship and service setting before selecting a route. The Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is relevant to violence and abuse within its defined relationships; not every adult concern is governed by that framework.

The Orange Door provides access to family-violence and family-support services. NDIS and aged-care providers have their own incident and regulatory obligations. A referral for support, a reportable incident and an application for a protective order are different actions.

Local pathway:
Hear the adult safely and identify immediate danger, coercion and practical dependence.
Identify whether the concern involves family violence, a disability or aged-care provider, another service or crime.
Use the relevant specialist, police and regulatory routes, checking any mandatory reporting duty.
Plan safe contact, practical support and follow-up without assuming that a referral authorises coercive action.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the appropriate complaint, advocacy or court route for the issue. OPA can provide information about decision-making and rights within its remit. Keep the adult’s wishes and the legal authority for any intervention visible, including where agencies disagree.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/family-violence-protection-act-2008
https://www.orangedoor.vic.gov.au/
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 distinguishes protection grounds and mandatory reporting. The mandatory-reporter categories depend on the role: do not assume every person called a social worker is included solely by title. A social worker may fall within a listed role, such as school counselling or out-of-home care work.

DFFH guidance requires listed reporters who form the relevant reasonable belief in their work to report protection concerns involving physical injury or sexual abuse. Other forms of significant harm may also be reported. The child’s harm and parental protection must be considered; the statutory reporting duty is not identical to every possible wellbeing concern.

Local pathway:
Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty.
Report to Child Protection as soon as practicable where the duty is engaged, including new grounds arising later.
Consider a support referral to The Orange Door where appropriate, without substituting it for a required protection report.
Check separate police and organisational duties, and plan child participation, cultural support and continuity.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the Child Protection process and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. DFFH guidance distinguishes reporting routes from family-support referrals. Advice within an organisation should not delay an applicable personal reporting obligation.

Sources:
https://providers.dffh.vic.gov.au/mandatory-reporting
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/children-youth-and-families-act-2005

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 requires covered public authorities to act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights, subject to statutory exceptions. Identify whether the provider is a public authority for the function involved. A Charter statement should explain the affected rights and reasoning, not simply declare compliance.

The Equal Opportunity Act 2010, Health Records Act 2001 and Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 have different scopes. Commonwealth law may also apply. Determine the organisation and information involved before selecting a privacy or discrimination pathway.

Local pathway:
Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority.
Consider the actual impact, alternatives and any lawful basis for limiting a right.
Arrange accessible and culturally safe participation and address applicable equality obligations.
Check the relevant privacy regime and explain access, correction, complaints and review.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission explains Charter duties and discrimination. Privacy and health complaints use their respective bodies and statutory routes. Obtain advice about the remedy for an alleged Charter breach rather than promising that every concern has a standalone Charter claim.

Sources:
https://www.humanrights.vic.gov.au/for-public-sector/charter-responsibilities/charter-and-the-government/
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/charter-human-rights-and-responsibilities-act-2006
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/health-records-act-2001

studentPathwaySteps.title: Children, Families and Transitions
studentPathwaySteps.task: Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming all social-work job titles create the same reporting duty, or confusing voluntary support with a mandatory report.

studentPathwaySteps.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
studentPathwaySteps.task: Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming every private provider has identical Charter duties or that naming rights establishes proper consideration.

scope: Learning guide with source-led exercises; not an exhaustive statement of law or an official professional assessment.
